title: What a king is for
hook: Krishna answers: a king in Magadha holds kings captive, and a ruler's first duty is to protect
carry: raja dharma: a leader's first duty is to protect

segments.voice: Yesterday: everyone in the sabha said yes, and Yudhishthira sent for Krishna anyway. Your line was krishna, the friend who sees further.

Krishna comes straight from Dwaraka, and Yudhishthira lays it all out. My father's wish. The sacrifice. My ministers say yes, my brothers say yes. But you'll tell me the truth: should I perform the Rajasuya? And Krishna does. You have every quality it takes, he says. Then comes the but. There's a king in Magadha. While he lives, this can't be done.
screen: `KRISHNA COMES.` → `SHOULD I DO THIS?` → `YES. BUT THERE'S A KING IN MAGADHA.`

segments.voice: First, what Yudhishthira is asking for. The Rajasuya is the great royal sacrifice, the one Harishchandra performed. A king who completes it is honored by other kings as sovereign over them, so other rulers have to come, and bow, and bring gifts. That's exactly the problem Krishna names. The king is Jarasandha of Magadha. Many kings already bow to him. Worse, he has captured kings in battle and holds them shut up in his mountain city, meaning to offer them as a sacrifice to Mahadeva. While those kings sit in his prison, Krishna says, no one else can claim to be honored by the kings of the earth. And Krishna tells it as someone hurt by it: fearing Jarasandha, his own people, the Yadavas, left Mathura for Dwaraka. Now look at what his counsel does. Yudhishthira asked, am I worthy of the honor? Krishna answers, what about the people in that prison? That's a teaching the epic comes back to again and again: raja dharma, the dharma of a king. In Hindu teaching, a ruler isn't there to be honored. He's there to protect, above all the ones who can't protect themselves. Jarasandha is the picture of the opposite: a king who uses people, even as offerings. So before anyone can be honored, someone has to be set free. Many teachers read it as a question for anyone who leads, a family, a team, a class: whom are you protecting? Tomorrow, Yudhishthira very nearly gives the whole thing up.
screen: `A SACRIFICE THAT MAKES A SOVEREIGN.` · `JARASANDHA OF MAGADHA.` · `WHAT ABOUT THE PRISONERS?` · `RAJA DHARMA: A KING PROTECTS.` · then, large: `FIRST, SOMEONE HAS TO BE SET FREE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people who depend on you in any way: a younger sibling, a friend, a team, a parent getting older. Name them one by one. If you pray, ask God to protect each one, and to help you protect them. If you don't, hold each name for a breath and ask what looking out for them would mean this week.
The Rajasuya. The great royal sacrifice that makes a king sovereign over kings, and that Krishna says can't happen while Jarasandha holds kings captive.
Your line: raja dharma, a leader's first duty is to protect. Before the honor, a prison door. Day seven hundred fifty-two, done.

howItsDone: The Rajasuya belongs to the Vedic royal rites; in the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira's Rajasuya is the rite through which other kings recognize his rule at Indraprastha.
